params.name: S1.1
params.hypothesis: Ink-amount meter: Its maps are a blurred copy of the digit's ink: every inked pixel raises the map around it, wherever it is and whichever way the stroke runs, so its average response measures how much ink the digit has. So thickening the strokes should raise it strongly, while a stroke of the same length should add about the same wherever it is placed and whichever way it runs. Self-probe: Thicken every stroke by one pixel (dilation) vs move the digit one pixel right: +1.45 SD against the control (95% interval +1.43 to +1.47, 1000 images; predicted up): agrees. A 10-pixel horizontal stroke along the top of the digit vs the same stroke upright along its right edge: +0.01 SD against the control (95% interval +0.00 to +0.02, 1000 images; predicted no change): agrees. Behaviour (the conclusion): It fires on most 0s (82%), 2s (72%), 8s (67%) and 3s (65%) and rarely on 1s (4%). Within each digit, the larger the amount of ink (ink pixels), the stronger the response (Spearman r = +0.99 averaged over digits; partial r = +0.99 with the digit held fixed). Concept check: Named concepts that also hold within digits, with the ink held fixed: a lot of ink (more: fires on 98% of images with it vs 7% without, same digit). The behaviour above is the reading; the concepts are a cross-check. Status: proven: every self-probe agrees (a directional one by at least 0.3 SD), and the reading holds within digits with the ink held fixed.

params.name: S2.1
params.hypothesis: Horizontal-stroke detector: It reads S1.2's blurred ink map and responds along horizontal strokes: the bars and flat curves at the top, middle and bottom of a digit. Upright strokes give it little. So a horizontal stroke should raise it more than the same stroke drawn upright, and making the digit wider should raise it more than making it taller by the same factor. The digit stretched 30% wider vs 30% taller: +0.72 SD against the control (95% interval +0.70 to +0.74, 1000 images; predicted up): agrees. Behaviour (the conclusion): It fires on most 3s (90%), 5s (86%), 2s (85%) and 0s (75%) and rarely on 1s (0%) and 4s (14%). Within each digit, the larger the amount of horizontal-stroke edge, the stronger the response (Spearman r = +0.62 averaged over digits; partial r = +0.45 with the digit and the ink count held fixed). params.name: S2.2
params.hypothesis: Lowest-stroke detector: It reads S2.1's horizontal-stroke map (and S1.1's ink map) and keeps the digit's lowest horizontal stroke, a horizontal stroke with no ink below it: the flat base of a 2, the bottom curve of a 0, 3, 5 or 6. It does not depend on where the digit sits in the image; ink below the stroke takes it away. So a horizontal stroke along the bottom of the digit should raise it far more than the same stroke along its top. A detached stroke drawn just below a digit that already ends in a horizontal stroke (0, 2, 3, 5) should lower it, because the old base now has ink below it, while the same stroke below a digit that ends in a stem (1, 4, 7, 9) should raise it, because it becomes the lowest stroke; the control is the same stroke drawn just above the digit. Self-probe: A 10-pixel horizontal stroke along the bottom of the digit vs the same stroke along its top: +0.81 SD against the control (95% interval +0.78 to +0.85, 1000 images; predicted up): agrees. On 0s, 2s, 3s and 5s, a 10-pixel horizontal stroke 3 pixels below the digit vs the same stroke 3 pixels above it: -0.88 SD against the control (95% interval -0.95 to -0.81, 390 images; predicted down): agrees. On 1s, 4s, 7s and 9s, the same stroke below vs above the digit: -0.24 SD against the control (95% interval -0.28 to -0.20, 413 images; predicted up): contradicts. An earlier prediction, that erasing the bottom quarter of the digit lowers it more than erasing as many ink pixels from the top quarter, failed (+0.05 SD): erasing the bottom of a 4 or 9 leaves its crossbar or loop as the new lowest stroke, which raises it. The reading was rewritten from 'a stroke along the bottom' to 'the lowest horizontal stroke' and probed again. Behaviour (the conclusion): It fires on most 2s (93%), 0s (89%), 3s (86%), 5s (85%) and 6s (76%) and rarely on 1s (0%), 9s (4%) and 4s (9%). Within each digit, the larger the amount of ink in the bottom quarter of the digit's box, the stronger the response (Spearman r = +0.75 averaged over digits; partial r = +0.59 with the digit and the ink count held fixed). Concept check: Named concepts that also hold within digits, with the ink held fixed: wide (more: fires on 65% of images with it vs 40% without, same digit); tall stem (less: fires on 17% of images with it vs 39% without, same digit). The behaviour above is the reading; the concepts are a cross-check. Status: contested: a self-probe went against the prediction.

params.name: S3.1
params.hypothesis: Central-band ink meter: It adds up the ink in a central upright band of the image (about columns 7 to 19, top to bottom); ink further out to the left or right counts little. So for the same amount of ink, a narrow upright digit fires it more than a wide one. So making the digit 30% wider should lower it compared with making it 30% taller (both add the same ink), and turning the digit on its side should lower it compared with mirroring it. Self-probe: The digit stretched 30% wider vs 30% taller: -0.45 SD against the control (95% interval -0.46 to -0.43, 1000 images; predicted down): agrees. The digit turned 90 degrees vs mirrored left to right: -0.52 SD against the control (95% interval -0.55 to -0.49, 1000 images; predicted down): agrees. params.name: root
params.hypothesis: Digit scores from the structures: The ten scores are exact sums: a constant plus one term per structure that feeds the score maps (and one for the image directly), each a kernel on the structure's exits, averaged over the map and mixed by the head (largest reconstruction error 2.1e-14). A digit can be recognised because a structure fires for it, or because a structure stays silent for it: the silence keeps a rival digit's score down. On 4s, a horizontal stroke along the top vs along the bottom (the '4' score margin): -1.36 SD against the control (95% interval -1.60 to -1.13, 97 images; predicted down): agrees. structures.name: S1
structures.title: Shared ink measure
structures.hypothesis: Shared ink measure: S1.1 and S1.2 both read the image and run in parallel. Their main exits agree almost exactly (r = 0.995), so the pair hands one measure, how much ink the digit has, to most later structures (S2, S3, S4, S5, S6 and S8) through different exits. The combination adds no new behaviour: a 10-class classifier on both children's pooled exits reaches 44% (cross-validated), against 36% for the better child alone. Self-probe: Thicken every stroke by one pixel (dilation) vs move the digit one pixel right: +1.45 SD against the control (95% interval +1.43 to +1.47, 1000 images; predicted up): agrees. Thicken every stroke by one pixel (dilation) vs move the digit one pixel right: +1.54 SD against the control (95% interval +1.52 to +1.56, 1000 images; predicted up): agrees. Both children respond to thicker strokes in the same way, as one ink measure would. Behaviour (the conclusion): Its main exit (h119, from S1.1): it fires on most 0s (82%), 2s (72%), 8s (67%) and 3s (65%) and rarely on 1s (4%). Concept check: No concept in the library matches within digits with the ink held fixed (the closest is tall stem: 20% with it vs 56% without, same digit, partial r = +0.01). Status: proven: every self-probe on the children agrees (a directional one by at least 0.3 SD).

superseded.title: 4-vs-7 separator (S1)

Together they separate 4s from 7s (76% balanced accuracy, cross-validated) much better than the best part alone (S1.2: 65%). Its strongest exit (map h119): correlates with 0s, 2s, 3s, 5s, 6s and 8s; mechanism unknown: no image rule explains it within digits (closest: a tall vertical stem, s = -0.68). It fires on 0s (87%), 2s (78%), 8s (74%), 3s (72%), 6s (65%) and 5s (59%). structures.name: S2
structures.title: Horizontal strokes, then the lowest one
structures.hypothesis: Horizontal strokes, then the lowest one: S2.1 finds horizontal strokes anywhere in the digit; S2.2 reads S2.1's map (with S1.1's ink map) and keeps the lowest one, the stroke with no ink below it (S2.1 feeds S2.2). What the combination adds is location: a stroke along the bottom instead of the top moves S2.2 by +0.81 SD but S2.1 by only +0.10 SD. A 10-class classifier on both children's pooled exits reaches 68% (cross-validated), against 53% for the better child alone. Self-probe: A horizontal stroke along the bottom vs the top (S2.2): +0.81 SD against the control (95% interval +0.78 to +0.85, 1000 images; predicted up): agrees. The same edit (S2.1): +0.10 SD against the control (95% interval +0.08 to +0.13, 1000 images; predicted no change): agrees. Behaviour (the conclusion): Its main exit (h11, from S2.1): it fires on most 3s (90%), 5s (86%), 2s (85%) and 0s (75%) and rarely on 1s (0%) and 4s (14%). Concept check: Named concepts that also hold within digits, with the ink held fixed: wide (more: fires on 76% of images with it vs 32% without, same digit); tall stem (less: fires on 11% of images with it vs 48% without, same digit). The behaviour above is the reading; the concepts are a cross-check. Status: proven: every self-probe on the children agrees (a directional one by at least 0.3 SD).

superseded.title: 3-vs-5 separator (S2)
superseded.hypothesis: 3-vs-5 separator (S2): Combines S2.1 (No-stem detector (S2.1)) and S2.2 (No-stem detector (S2.2)). S2.1 feeds S2.2. structures.name: S4
structures.title: Left-of-centre stroke detector
structures.hypothesis: Left-of-centre stroke detector: It counts ink in an upright band just left of the image centre (about columns 8 to 11, mid-height) and counts ink further left (columns 0 to 6) against it. It fires when the digit has an upright stroke on its left side near the middle, as the left side of a 0 or 6 does, and stays low when the left side is open, as in a 3 or 7. structures.name: S5
structures.title: Top-bar detector
structures.hypothesis: Top-bar detector: It responds to a horizontal stroke across the top of the digit (image rows about 4 to 9, central columns), as in a 2, 3, 5 or 7. Ink across the middle rows holds it back, and a stroke at the bottom raises it a little. So a horizontal stroke along the top of the digit should raise it far more than the same stroke along the bottom, and erasing the top quarter of the digit should lower it more than erasing as many ink pixels from the bottom quarter. The behaviour above is the reading; the concepts are a cross-check. Status: proven: every self-probe agrees (a directional one by at least 0.3 SD), and the reading holds within digits with the ink held fixed.

structures.title: Flat and falling strokes of wide digits

structures.name: S7
structures.title: Low-crossbar detector
structures.hypothesis: Low-crossbar detector: It reads S2.1's and S6.2's horizontal-stroke maps and weighs them by height: horizontal ink in the lower half of the image, right of centre, raises it, and ink near the very top of the image (above about row 7) lowers it. annotations.name: root
annotations.title: Digit scores from the structures
annotations.hypothesis: Digit scores from the structures: The ten scores are exact sums: a constant plus one term per structure that feeds the score maps (and one for the image directly), each a kernel on the structure's exits, averaged over the map and mixed by the head (largest reconstruction error 2.1e-14). A digit can be recognised because a structure fires for it, or because a structure stays silent for it: the silence keeps a rival digit's score down. So waking a structure that a digit needs silent (drawing the stroke it detects) should lower that digit's score margin more than drawing the same stroke where the structure does not see it. Self-probe: On the probe images the same structure comes first for 8 of the 10 digits. On 1s, a 10-pixel horizontal stroke across the middle vs the same stroke drawn along the 1 (the '1' score margin): -3.03 SD against the control (95% interval -3.28 to -2.78, 113 images; predicted down): agrees. On 6s, a horizontal stroke along the top vs along the bottom (the '6' score margin): -5.50 SD against the control (95% interval -5.98 to -5.02, 99 images; predicted down): agrees. On 4s, a horizontal stroke along the top vs along the bottom (the '4' score margin): -1.36 SD against the control (95% interval -1.60 to -1.13, 97 images; predicted down): agrees. On 3s, an upright stroke along the left edge vs along the right edge (the '3' score margin): -3.69 SD against the control (95% interval -3.94 to -3.46, 102 images; predicted down): agrees. Behaviour (the conclusion): Which structure each digit depends on most (discovery images): 0s on S8 (Upright-stroke detector), which fires on 92% of them (holding its term at the average costs 29% of 0s, most of them to '6'); 1s on S2 (Horizontal strokes, then the lowest one), which is silent (below its median response) on 100% of them (holding its term at the average costs 92% of 1s, most of them to '6'); 2s on S2 (Horizontal strokes, then the lowest one), which fires on 85% of them (holding its term at the average costs 18% of 2s, most of them to '7'); 3s on S4 (Left-of-centre stroke detector), which is silent (below its median response) on 99% of them (holding its term at the average costs 66% of 3s, most of them to '5'); 4s on S5 (Top-bar detector), which is silent (below its median response) on 99% of them (holding its term at the average costs 70% of 4s, most of them to '7'); 5s on S6 (Flat and falling strokes of wide digits), which fires on 86% of them (holding its term at the average costs 15% of 5s, most of them to '2'); 6s on S5 (Top-bar detector), which is silent (below its median response) on 99% of them (holding its term at the average costs 86% of 6s, most of them to '5'); 7s on S5 (Top-bar detector), which fires on 97% of them (holding its term at the average costs 32% of 7s, most of them to '4'); 8s on S7 (Low-crossbar detector), which is silent (below its median response) on 95% of them (holding its term at the average costs 18% of 8s, most of them to '2'); 9s on S4 (Left-of-centre stroke detector), which is silent (below its median response) on 92% of them (holding its term at the average costs 35% of 9s, most of them to '5').
